title: Grade 7 Science — Wed, May 27
description: Nutrition in Plants — Day 3 of 5: Leaf structure and minerals
subject: science

questions.question: Why do plants need minerals in addition to glucose from photosynthesis?
options: Minerals are needed for building proteins, DNA, chlorophyll, and other cell components
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes glucose (energy + carbon). But plants also need nitrogen (proteins), phosphorus (DNA/ATP), magnesium (chlorophyll), etc. — all from minerals.

questions.question: A plant shows yellowing of leaves (chlorosis). This is likely due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and magnesium are essential for chlorophyll production. Their deficiency causes pale/yellow leaves (chlorosis).

questions.question: What is the spongy mesophyll layer in a leaf designed for?
options: Gas exchange — loose cells allow CO₂ and O₂ to move through air spaces
questions.explanation: The spongy mesophyll has loosely packed cells with air spaces, facilitating the movement of CO₂ (in) and O₂ (out).

questions.question: The palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts because:
options: They are the primary photosynthesis cells, directly under the leaf surface to receive maximum light
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are tall, tightly packed cells directly below the upper epidermis. Their high chloroplast density maximises photosynthesis.

questions.question: The waxy cuticle on the upper leaf surface prevents:
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is waterproof and reduces transpiration (water loss). It also protects against some pests.

questions.question: Why are most stomata on the UNDERSIDE (lower surface) of leaves?
options: To reduce water loss — shaded side is cooler and less directly exposed to sun
Roots are closer to the underside
questions.explanation: Stomata on the underside are in shade and cooler air, which reduces water loss compared to having them on the sun-exposed top.

questions.question: Transpiration is:
options: Transport of food from leaves to other parts
Loss of water vapour from plant surfaces (mainly leaves through stomata)
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour through stomata and leaf surfaces. It also creates a 'pull' that helps draw water up from roots.

questions.question: Leguminous plants (peas, beans) have a special ability regarding nitrogen. What is it?
options: They release nitrogen gas into the air
They have bacteria in their root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrates
They absorb nitrogen directly from air through stomata
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of legumes fix N₂ (from air) into ammonia/nitrates — enriching the soil and providing nitrogen to the plant.

questions.question: The food made in leaves is transported to other parts of the plant through:
questions.explanation: Phloem vessels transport the sugars (food) made in leaves to all other parts of the plant — roots, stems, fruits.

questions.question: A plant is growing in soil lacking phosphorus. Which would be most affected?
options: Root growth and energy storage (ATP formation)
questions.explanation: Phosphorus is essential for DNA, ATP (energy currency), and cell membranes. Deficiency stunts root growth and weakens energy metabolism.

questions.question: At night, which of these occurs in green plants?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires light and STOPS at night. Respiration (breaking down glucose for energy) continues 24 hours.

questions.question: In very bright light, why do stomata sometimes close?
options: To prevent wilting by reducing water loss when light is very intense and temperature high
questions.explanation: In very bright or hot conditions, plants close stomata to prevent excessive water loss, even at the cost of slowing photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes xylem and phloem?
options: Xylem carries water up; Phloem carries food both up and down
Phloem carries water; Xylem carries food
questions.explanation: Xylem: water and minerals travel upward only (from roots). Phloem: sugars travel in both directions — from leaves to roots, stems, fruits.

questions.question: Excess glucose in leaves is stored as:
questions.explanation: Excess glucose made during photosynthesis is converted to starch for storage in leaves, roots, and seeds.

questions.question: A plant in a sealed transparent box over time: which gas increases inside the box during daylight?
questions.explanation: During daytime, photosynthesis releases O₂. This would accumulate inside the sealed box, increasing oxygen levels.
